input:
An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 45 days at 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 85% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.8 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured; solvent loss was 1.3 kg per tonne captured.

Amine absorption separates carbon dioxide from a gas stream by contact with an amine solvent, which takes up the carbon dioxide from the gas. The capture percentage takes the carbon dioxide in the treated gas as its whole: it is the part of that carbon dioxide which the solvent removed, and the part not captured leaves the unit with the treated gas. The capture figure is the share of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas that the solvent took up. Steam demand and solvent loss are stated on the same basis, per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, so the three results describe one run on one gas: capture states what the unit removed, steam demand states the heat the removal consumed, and solvent loss states the solvent the run consumed with it.

The test conditions bound every figure. The gas came from a cement kiln, the unit was a pilot unit rather than a full-scale plant, and the run held one treated rate for its whole length. No result describes a different gas, a larger unit, or a longer campaign.

Beyond 45 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested. The figures therefore stand for 45 days of pilot operation on kiln gas, and the solvent's behaviour under longer exposure to kiln dust is not known.
